Summary Answer
Thriving at work—defined as simultaneously experiencing high vitality (energy and positive affect) and perceiving learning and growth—consistently predicts higher levels of innovative work behavior (IWB), including generating new ideas, spotting problems, and implementing improvements within roles and units. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Empirical work reports that when individuals experience more thriving, they are more likely to have the motivation to engage in innovative behavior and to go beyond their regular responsibilities</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Prior reviews argue thriving differs from intrinsic motivation yet is linked to innovative behavior by increasing employees’ functionality and adaptability</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">An independent samples test in railway employees found higher IWB among employees scoring high versus low on thriving, with learning better predicting IWB than vitality</cite>. Mechanistically, thriving’s learning facet sharpens problem detection and solution-building, while vitality supplies the energy and broadened thought–action repertoire to try out novel ideas; these processes are amplified by organizational support for innovation and leadership that fosters trust and psychological safety. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">An integrative account is that thriving increases motivation and adaptability, enabling employees to implement new processes</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Positive affect broadens thought–action repertoire and enhances creative problem solving; vitality contributes to motivation</cite>. Contextual enablers such as transformational leadership, intellectual humility, and connectivity strengthen the thriving→IWB link, while weak support can attenuate it. <cite id="ffbba37e-0">In a Saudi sample (n=224), transformational leadership increased thriving, which fully mediated its effect on IWB</cite> <cite id="ffbba37e-4">Leadership that fosters trust and support reduces stress and provides psychological safety, stimulating vitality and learning motivation and enhancing thriving</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Carmeli and Spreitzer note thriving relates to the work environment; organizational support for innovation facilitates innovative behavior</cite>.

What Thriving Is and How It Is Measured
Thriving at work is a psychological state comprising vitality (energy and enthusiasm) and learning (acquiring new knowledge and skills), both required at high levels to “thrive.” <cite id="a736492a-0">It is defined as employees’ joint sense of vitality and learning; contextual resources and climates promote agentic behaviors such as exploration that lead to thriving; and thriving relates positively to health, attitudes, and performance</cite> <cite id="a736492a-3">Vitality is enthusiasm and motivation; learning is knowledge acquisition and self-confidence building; two-factor models fit better than single-factor alternatives</cite>. The 10-item Work Thriving Scale (Porath et al., 2012) measures vitality (items 6–10) and learning (items 1–5) on 5–7 point Likert scales, with strong reliability in multiple languages and samples. <cite id="a736492a-1">The scale has two 5-item subscales (learning and vitality), often summed (range 10–70); in one study Cronbach’s alpha was 0.902 overall with 0.776 and 0.873 for learning and vitality</cite> <cite id="a736492a-2">A Korean adaptation used a 5-point scale with excellent reliability (α = 0.93)</cite> <cite id="a736492a-4">The instrument is commonly scored via subscale totals or averages; in one study α = 0.907</cite>. Meta-analytic syntheses show thriving is positively associated with performance-related outcomes such as organizational citizenship and creativity, situating IWB as part of this broader performance constellation. <cite id="a736492a-0">A meta-analysis found positive relationships between thriving and task performance, organizational citizenship, subjective health, burnout, job satisfaction, commitment, and turnover intention</cite>.

Direct Impact: Thriving and Innovative Work Behavior
Multiple empirical studies and reviews report a positive association between thriving and IWB. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Innovative work behavior involves proposing new ideas, detecting problems, and implementing improvements; empirical work supports a positive link between thriving and innovative behavior</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">The literature supports that thriving sparks innovative behavior and increases functionality and adaptability; hypotheses posit a positive thriving→IWB link</cite>. In applied settings, higher thriving is associated with higher IWB, and facet-level analyses often find learning to be a stronger predictor than vitality alone. <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Railway employees high in thriving showed significantly higher IWB; learning better predicted IWB than vitality</cite>. Cross-cultural work from Chinese samples likewise finds thriving positively related to organizational support for innovation and IWB, reinforcing generality beyond Western contexts. <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Hypotheses in a Chinese perspective posit a positive relation between thriving and organizational support for innovation, with prior research indicating thriving facilitates innovative behavior</cite>. Conceptual accounts emphasize that vitality supplies energy and motivation, while learning equips employees to recognize problems and craft creative solutions, jointly fostering proactive innovation. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Thriving differs from intrinsic motivation; vitality and learning jointly drive motivation and adaptability for innovative behavior</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Positive affect broadens thought–action repertoire, enhancing creative thinking and problem solving; vitality contributes to motivation</cite>.

Mechanisms Linking Thriving to Innovation
Two complementary mechanisms are well supported. First, the learning facet of thriving. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Learning and development at work enable employees to recognize problems and implement improvements, a core driver of innovative behavior</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Learning better predicts IWB than vitality, consistent with thriving’s learning-to-creativity pathway</cite>. Second, the vitality mechanism. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Vitality supplies the energy to seek out and implement new processes and solutions, supported by psychological and social resources that facilitate thriving</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Positive emotions broaden thought–action repertoire and enhance problem-solving, supporting novel idea generation and experimentation</cite>. A third pathway channels thriving into IWB through organizational support for innovation. <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Organizational support of innovation facilitates innovative behavior and is hypothesized to mediate the link from thriving to IWB</cite> <cite id="a736492a-0">Socially embedded theory posits that contextual resources and trust/respect climates enable agentic behaviors that build thriving and performance</cite>. Leadership behaviors that build trust, connectivity, and psychological safety further translate thriving into innovation by buffering stress and stimulating learning and vitality. <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Leadership and organizational strategies can divert individual functionality toward innovative behavior, though empirical support has historically been limited</cite> <cite id="ffbba37e-4">Intellectual humility leadership fosters trust and support, reducing stress, increasing psychological safety, and enhancing vitality and learning motivation, thereby boosting thriving</cite>.

Role of Leadership and Context
Leadership styles that broaden employee agency (e.g., transformational, intellectually humble) reliably bolster thriving and its downstream innovation effects. <cite id="ffbba37e-0">In private sector employees in Saudi Arabia, transformational leadership increased thriving and thriving fully mediated its effect on IWB</cite>. Across cultures, organizational support for innovation, supervisor support, and team connectivity are key enablers. <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Prior research shows organizational support of innovation facilitates innovative behavior; thriving is related to the work environment</cite> <cite id="a736492a-3">Supervisor support and psychological capital positively impact thriving, per socially embedded models</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Trust and connectivity are sources of thriving, which in turn sparks innovative behavior</cite>. Conversely, in contexts low on support or high on hindrance stressors, the thriving→IWB link is weaker, highlighting a contingent relationship. <cite id="a736492a-3">Challenge stressors can bolster thriving via affect and motivation pathways, whereas hindrance stressors undermine resources; empirical studies show thriving relates to a wide range of positive attitudes and performance outcomes, implying dependence on supportive climates</cite>.

Distinguishing Thriving from Intrinsic Motivation and Other Resources
Thriving is distinct from simple intrinsic motivation but synergistic with it: vitality and learning co-create a state that energizes and skillfully enables innovation. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Thriving differs from intrinsic motivation, combining vitality with a learning impetus for goal achievement and recognition</cite>. Measurement work cautions that summing vitality and learning can miss the simultaneous-experience requirement central to thriving, underscoring the need to assess both facets together when linking to innovation outcomes. <cite id="a736492a-0">Operationalizing thriving as average or sum scores may be problematic because it does not represent the simultaneous high levels of vitality and learning that constitute thriving</cite>.

Practical Implications for Cultivating Innovative Work Behavior
- Invest in learning-and-feedback systems that make growth salient and teachable; pair with autonomy-supportive leadership to build vitality and psychological safety. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Thriving improves adaptability and effectiveness at work, supporting innovation</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Organizational support for innovation facilitates innovative behavior</cite> <cite id="ffbba37e-4">Leadership that fosters trust and safety stimulates vitality and learning motivation, enhancing thriving</cite>.
- Track thriving using validated 10-item scales by vitality and learning to diagnose where to intervene (e.g., energy drains vs. skill stagnation). <cite id="a736492a-1">The Work Thriving Scale offers reliable learning and vitality subscales</cite> <cite id="a736492a-2">High internal consistency is observed in adapted versions</cite>.
- Design work and processes that create frequent “innovation loops” (observe problems→learn→try→reflect), and explicitly recognize and resource prototypes to translate learning into implementation. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Thriving fuels motivation and adaptability to implement new processes</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Learning better predicts IWB; vitality contributes to motivation for proactive innovation</cite>.

Limitations and Evidence Gaps
Most studies are cross-sectional, limiting causal inference; however, mediation and moderation models plus sectoral and cross-cultural replication strengthen inference. <cite id="ffbba37e-0">Cross-sectional SEM showed full mediation of leadership→IWB via thriving</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Reviews note few empirical tests but growing evidence that thriving promotes innovative behavior</cite>. Future work should prioritize longitudinal designs linking changes in thriving to subsequent innovation outputs, experimentally manipulating thriving or its antecedents (e.g., autonomy, feedback, trust interventions), and mapping differential contributions of vitality vs. learning across roles (e.g., knowledge vs. routine-intensive jobs).

Bottom Line
Thriving at work reliably elevates innovative work behavior by energizing employees to seek and test novel ideas while simultaneously equipping them with learning and psychological resources to implement solutions; effects are strongest when leadership and organizational support for innovation create trust, safety, and developmental resources. <cite id="8637d2b4-0">Empirical links between thriving and innovative behavior are supported</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-3">Applied tests show higher IWB with higher thriving and learning’s stronger predictive role</cite> <cite id="ffbba37e-0">Leadership can fully channel effects through thriving</cite> <cite id="8637d2b4-1">Support for innovation and trust/connectivity are key contextual enablers</cite> <cite id="a736492a-0">Meta-analytic syntheses situate thriving as a broad driver of positive performance and well-being outcomes, including creativity</cite>.

Title: Thriving at work: an investigation of the independent and joint effects of vitality and learning on employee health
Snippet: Thriving at work has been defined as employees' joint sense of vitality and learning (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Accordingly, employees who are thriving feel active and strong (i.e., vitality) and, at the same time, believe that they are acquiring new knowledge and skills (i.e., learning). To experience thriving, both vitality and learning have to be present at high levels (Spreitzer et al., 2005). In developing their socially embedded model of thriving at work, Spreitzer et al. (2005) explain how contextual features of the work environment (e.g., climates of trust and respect) and resources (e.g., knowledge, support) promote agentic employee behaviours (e.g., exploration, task focus) that ultimately lead to thriving. Moreover, the model assumes that physical and mental health, as well as selfdevelopment, are key outcomes of thriving (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Since the introduction of Spreitzer et al.'s (2005) model and the development of self-report measures to assess vitality and learning (e.g., Porath et al., 2012), thriving at work has attracted considerable research interest. Synthesizing this literature, a meta-analysis reported positive relationships between overall thriving at work and various health-related (e.g., subjective health, burnout), attitudinal (e.g., job satisfaction, commitment), and performance-related outcomes (e.g., task performance, organizational citizenship; Kleine et al., 2019). 

In empirical studies, thriving at work has been operationalized using either average or sum scores of ratings on separate vitality and learning scales (e.g., Carmeli & Spreitzer, 2009;Porath et al., 2012), or by assessing the effects of vitality and learning as two predictors that each constitute part of the thriving construct (e.g., Marchiondo et al., 2018). The use of average and sum scores may be problematic for the study of thriving at work, because this operationalization does not represent the experience of simultaneously high levels of vitality and learning (Kleine et al., 2019).
</snippet>

Thriving at work is a kind of growth gauge that provides a sense to the individual of how he/she is doing (Porath et al. 2012) in relation to developing new proficiencies and working with energy (Kark and Carmeli 2009). It captures the joint experience of vitality and learning at work, but differs from intrinsic motivation (Spreitzer et al. 2005). According to social cognitive theory, all individuals need to build positive resources to increase their adaptability (Spreitzer et al. 2012). The literature supports the argument that thriving sparks innovative behavior (Amabile et al. 1996;Carmeli and Spreitzer 2009;Spreitzer et al. 2005;Wallace et al. 2016). Moreover, it increases individuals' functionality and adaptability (Mumford et al. 2002;Niessen et al. 2012;Scott and Bruce 1994). Carmeli and Spreitzer (2009) noted that thriving is related to the work environment. 

Individual thriving consists of energy involving positive emotion and eagerness to engage in a particular task (Dutton 2003); moreover, the work environment can motivate the employee to go beyond the job responsibilities and think creatively. Prior research shows that organizational support of innovation facilitates innovative behavior (Gilson and Shalley 2004;Kark and Carmeli 2009). Patterson et al. (2004) added that innovative work is not passive-it needs energy to seek out new technologies, processes, techniques, and products with support from the team and management to accept new ideas. Porath et al. (2012) mentioned that organizational strategies can divert the individual's functionality towards innovative behavior, but there is little empirical support for this claim. Based on the above analysis, we proposed the following hypothesis: H 1 . Thriving is positively related to organizational support for innovation (OSI).

snippet.text:
In business today, organizations need to maintain a thriving workforce through different strategies in order to remain competitive and sustain their performance (Prem et al. 2017;Walumbwa et al. 2018). Thriving involves "a psychological state in which individuals experience both a sense of vitality and a sense of learning at work" (Spreitzer et al. 2005) (p. 538). Previous studies considered thriving as a way to overcome burnout, absenteeism, disengagement, and stress (Fritz et al. 2011;Prem et al. 2017). Nevertheless, emerging research has suggested that thriving at work is also an important antecedent of positive organizational outcomes, such as improved job satisfaction, lower stress, and higher organizational commitment. Carmeli and Spreitzer (2009) examined the role of thriving at work and considered it as an essential element influencing innovative behavior. Research has further suggested that thriving at work depends on contextual factors in order to promote innovative behavior (Porath et al. 2012;Spreitzer et al. 2012). 

Scholars have highlighted many factors that enable and promote thriving at work. However, the role of supervisors, social connectivity, and individual characteristics has been understudied in previous studies (Carmeli and Spreitzer 2009;Walumbwa et al. 2018). Similarly, we know very little about the contextual factors of thriving at work and innovative behavior, and few studies examined the positive relation between the two variables (Carmeli and Spreitzer 2009;Jokisaari 2013;Kark and Carmeli 2009). Therefore, the process through which thriving may influence innovative behavior is not yet clearly understood (Wallace et al. 2016). We suggest that organizational support for innovation may be an important mediating mechanism that explains how a thriving workforce can be more encouraged to exhibit innovative behavior. 

Adm. Sci. 2018, 8, 46 2 of 14 As such, this study aimed to test social cognitive theory, which addresses the linkage between contextual effects on individual behavior, including intervening organizational variables. These variables may involve leadership, subordinates, and management support for innovation. Considerable evidence suggests that it is crucial to identify the social conditions and organizational strategies that influence individual behaviors (Madrid et al. 2014;Shanker et al. 2017).

Innovative work behavior (IWB) is based on new and useful ideas, process, or procedures that aim to achieve within a work role, group, or organization [14]. It includes problem detection or comes up with new ideas, solutions, and implementation. However, thriving serves as a gauge to monitor their own development and helps to improve the effectiveness and adaptability at work [2,3,12]. 

When individuals experience more thriving, they may be more likely to have the motivation to engage in innovative behavior [8,15,16] and go beyond their regular role as well as responsibilities. Sonenshein et al. [17] noted that thriving is distinct from intrinsic motivation, because of the vitality it derives as a desire to perform such behavior on effective enjoyment way and learning impetus of individual for goal achievement and personal recognition. 

According to previous studies, an individual's innovative behavior is related to learning and development at work which enables the employee to recognize problems and implement improvements [3,8]. In this process, an employee needs to learn the required expertise to understand the process, distinguish the problems, and find a creative solution [8]. Second, employees must be energetic to devote to implementing the new process, whereas psychological and social resources facilitate thriving and allow individuals' to be more innovative [3]. Previous empirical work supports the link between thriving and innovative behavior [8,12,18,19]. Thus, we hypothesize that H 1 : Thriving will be positively associated with innovative work behavior.

Title: Thriving at work: an investigation of the independent and joint effects of vitality and learning on employee health
Snippet: Thriving at work has been defined as employees' joint sense of vitality and learning (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Accordingly, employees who are thriving feel active and strong (i.e., vitality) and, at the same time, believe that they are acquiring new knowledge and skills (i.e., learning). To experience thriving, both vitality and learning have to be present at high levels (Spreitzer et al., 2005). In developing their socially embedded model of thriving at work, Spreitzer et al. (2005) explain how contextual features of the work environment (e.g., climates of trust and respect) and resources (e.g., knowledge, support) promote agentic employee behaviours (e.g., exploration, task focus) that ultimately lead to thriving. Moreover, the model assumes that physical and mental health, as well as selfdevelopment, are key outcomes of thriving (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Since the introduction of Spreitzer et al.'s (2005) model and the development of self-report measures to assess vitality and learning (e.g., Porath et al., 2012), thriving at work has attracted considerable research interest. Synthesizing this literature, a meta-analysis reported positive relationships between overall thriving at work and various health-related (e.g., subjective health, burnout), attitudinal (e.g., job satisfaction, commitment), and performance-related outcomes (e.g., task performance, organizational citizenship; Kleine et al., 2019). 

In empirical studies, thriving at work has been operationalized using either average or sum scores of ratings on separate vitality and learning scales (e.g., Carmeli & Spreitzer, 2009;Porath et al., 2012), or by assessing the effects of vitality and learning as two predictors that each constitute part of the thriving construct (e.g., Marchiondo et al., 2018). The use of average and sum scores may be problematic for the study of thriving at work, because this operationalization does not represent the experience of simultaneously high levels of vitality and learning (Kleine et al., 2019).

Snippet: The Thriving at Work Scale was developed by Porath et al. (2012) [31] and translated and revised by Han et al. (2020) [40] to measure the level of Thriving at Work of employees, including two dimensions, the learning dimension (5 items) and the vitality dimension (5 items), with a total of 10 entries, each of which is scored on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree" on a scale of 1 to 7, with entries 4 and 8 being reverse-scored entries. The total score ranges from 10 to 70, with higher scores indicating a higher level of Thriving at Work. The Cronbach's alpha value for this scale is 0.771. The Cronbach's alpha coefficient of this scale in this study was 0.902 for the overall scale, and the Cronbach's alpha coefficients of the learning and vitality dimensions were 0.776 and 0.873, respectively.

Snippet: According to Spreitzer (2005), thriving at work refers to the psychological state that individuals experience both vitality and learning in their work at the same time. Spreitzer (2005) and Porath et al. (2012) developed and validated the construct of thriving at work, including "vitality" and "learning." Vitality is the state of enthusiasm and motivation in employees (Nix et al., 1999), and learning is the ability of employees to improve their level and build self-confidence through knowledge acquisition (Carver, 1998). Although each dimension indicates a certain degree of personal growth and development in work, it is only when the two dimensions are combined and achieve a high level that they can promote each other and form the experience of thriving at work (Porath et al., 2012). Some empirical studies showed that the two-factor model of thriving at work has a higher data fit than other structures (Carmeli and Spreitzer, 2011;Niessen et al., 2012). Many studies showed that thriving at work can be used as a measure of personal growth perception, which helps people to understand what they are doing and how they are doing (Paterson et al., 2014;Spreitzer, 2005). 

Existing studies have found that thriving at work is related to a wide range of positive effects on employees' attitudes, behavior, and performance.

According to Spreitzer (2005), thriving at work refers to the psychological state that individuals experience both vitality and learning in their work at the same time. Spreitzer (2005) and Porath et al. (2012) developed and validated the construct of thriving at work, including "vitality" and "learning." Vitality is the state of enthusiasm and motivation in employees (Nix et al., 1999), and learning is the ability of employees to improve their level and build self-confidence through knowledge acquisition (Carver, 1998). Although each dimension indicates a certain degree of personal growth and development in work, it is only when the two dimensions are combined and achieve a high level that they can promote each other and form the experience of thriving at work (Porath et al., 2012). Some empirical studies showed that the two-factor model of thriving at work has a higher data fit than other structures (Carmeli and Spreitzer, 2011;Niessen et al., 2012). Many studies showed that thriving at work can be used as a measure of personal growth perception, which helps people to understand what they are doing and how they are doing (Paterson et al., 2014;Spreitzer, 2005). 

Existing studies have found that thriving at work is related to a wide range of positive effects on employees' attitudes, behavior, and performance.

Title: Thriving at Work as a Mediator of the Relationship between Transformational Leadership and Innovative Work Behavior
Snippet: Thriving at work is a positive psychological state in which individuals experience a sense of vitality and learning. The purpose of this quantitative study is to examine the effect of transformational leadership on innovative work behavior and the mediating effect of thriving at work on the relationship between transformational leadership and innovative work behavior among private sector employees in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. A cross-sectional research design was used to collect data from 224 private sector employees. The results of the study reveal that transformational leadership is positively related to thriving at work and thriving at work is positively related to innovative work behavior. Furthermore, thriving at work fully mediates the relationship between transformational leadership and innovative work behavior. The theoretical and practical implications for are discussed.

Title: Development of thriving at work and organizational citizenship behavior through Islamic work ethics and humble leadership
Snippet: In the last 2 decades, the emergent concept of thriving at work has attracted management researchers. The concept of human thriving was initially used to describe human function and how humans develop and adapt to various situations (Brown et al., 2017). More specifically, thriving refers to the "joint experience of a sense of vitality and learning" (Porath et al., 2012: p. 250) experienced by a person in an environment. Regarding the context of the work environment, Kleine et al. (2019) identified thriving at work outcomes, including health (e.g., burnout), attitude (e.g., job satisfaction, turnover intention), and performance (e.g., organizational citizenship behavior and creativity). Due to its influence on various employee behaviors and attitudes, thriving at work is extremely important for companies in developing talent and employee health and well-being, as well as managing competitiveness (Pfeffer, 2010;Porath et al., 2012). 

A prior study widely adopted by researchers is the socially embedded thriving model developed by Spreitzer et al. (2005). In this model, Spreitzer et al. identified two main factors of thriving at work: contextual and resources. They also added agentic behavior (task focus and exploration) to explain that individuals can be internally motivated to thrive in their work. Furthermore, they stated that thriving at work improves individual health and well-being (Spreitzer et al., 2005). Recently, two meta-analyses (i.e., Kleine et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2021) expanded Spreitzer et al.'s model by identifying the antecedents and consequences of thriving at work in a broader manner. Despite numerous studies identifying the predictors of employees' thriving at work, several concepts have not yet been identified. For example, Liu et al. (2021) identified five leadership models (empowering, servant, authentic, leader-member exchange (LMX), and transformational leadership) as sources of thriving and ignored the recently popular leadership model, namely leader humility.

Snippet: Thriving is a positive subjective experience that helps individual guide and adjust their work contexts to achieve continued progress [14]. Thus, thriving is frequently considered as an important internal factor to evaluate individual growth and progress [25]. Employees who possess higher levels of thriving at work will typically achieve higher job performance than those with lower levels of thriving [15,25]. 

Thriving at work can be conceptualized as a psychological experience including two senses: learning and vitality [14]. Learning belongs to cognitive dimension, indicating a feeling of adding, and enables one to apply new knowledge and skills [14,33,34]. In contrast, vitality belongs to the affective dimension, denoting a positive feeling related to possessing enough energy [14,35]. To thrive at work, one must be both successful in achieving learning and vitality [14,36]. In other words, if employees think that they are gaining knowledge or skills, but do not feel alive, they are not thriving at work. Similarly, employees are not thriving when they only feel energized but do not engage in learning at work. 

In their seminal work, Spreitzer et al. [14] developed a socially embedded model to further study thriving at work. The model focuses on two types factors: unit work contextual features and resources produced in individuals work, which both boost the thriving of employees by affecting agentic work behaviors. Based on their research [14], more researchers have started to explore the antecedent of thriving at work. For instance, Paterson, Luthans, and Jeung [18] considered that supervisor support and psychological capital have a positive impact on thriving at work. Spreitzer and Porath [25] built an integrative model to explain how self-determination facilitates their thriving at work. Abid, et al. [37] investigated how to promote employees' thriving at work and reduce turnover intentions. Carmeli and Spreitzer [16] found that thriving at work is positively affected by trust and connectivity. Furthermore, thriving at work is also associated with some important individual and organization outcomes such as self-development, performance, health, adaptability, innovative behaviors, turnover intention, and even for home life [16,18,25,36,[38][39][40][41].
